title: How a small clinic should write an about page
metaTitle: How a small clinic should write an about page
excerpt: A clinic about page should name the people a patient will meet and why that matters to the visit. Skip the origin story unless it changes the decision to book.
alt: A two-lane road through red rock, with a single car far ahead and a mountain at the end, a path with a visible destination for an about page that should name who a patient is going to meet.
caption: A road through red rock, one car, a mountain ahead. The page should say who is at the end of the trip. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on a small clinic about page?
faqs.answer: The names and roles of the people a patient will meet, what each person does in the visit, and a way to book. Include the registration or credential that changes the decision, in plain language. Leave out a long origin story unless one fact in it would change whether this patient books.

faqs.question: Should we tell the founder's story?
faqs.answer: Tell it only when it helps the patient understand the care. A clinician who has done this work in this town for years is relevant. A childhood anecdote that does not change the visit is not. Put any story after the names, so a reader who leaves quickly has still seen who is responsible.

faqs.question: How should we handle staff who do not want to be photographed?
faqs.answer: Respect that. Name the role and describe the responsibility in type, and do not substitute a stock portrait. A missing photo with a true sentence is more trustworthy than a face that does not work at the clinic. Update the page when roles change, the same week if you can.

markdown:
A small clinic about page is proof that people stand behind the visit. Name who does the work, and say why a patient who is already anxious should care. Then offer a way to book.

Skip the origin myth unless a fact in it changes that decision. A story about why you founded the clinic does not, by itself, tell someone who will be in the room with them.

## Who they will meet

Open with the people in the order a patient meets them. The person on the desk. The clinician. Anyone else who will be in the room, such as a trainee, if trainees are sometimes present. Say that last part plainly. Discovering an extra person at the door is a harder surprise than reading it here.

Google's helpful-content guidance asks a "who" question that fits a clinic exactly. Is it obvious who is responsible, and can a reader learn more about those people? Health is one of the topics where Google says trust deserves extra weight. An about page that hides the clinicians behind a paragraph about "our family" fails the question. A name, a role, and a sentence about the visit answers it.

Use photographs from your rooms if you have consent. A clinician at the desk they actually use, or standing in the treatment room without performing for the camera. If someone declines a portrait, publish the role anyway. Do not buy a replacement face. Patients can tell, and the moment they suspect the face is borrowed, the names become suspect too.

Write what each person does, not what they love on weekends. Weekend detail can follow in a clause if the person wants it. It cannot lead. "Dr. Shah leads first visits for joint pain and writes the plan before you leave" is the sentence. The hobby is optional color after the patient knows they are in competent hands.

## Why an anxious patient should care

Relevance is the second job. A biography that could sit on a consultancy site has not said why someone in pain is reading. Connect the person to the hour the patient fears.

"Sam checks you in and explains the fee again before you sit down" tells a worried person the fee will not be an ambush. "Sam loves dogs" does not. "Dr. Shah will say if this clinic is the wrong place and will help with a referral" tells them they are allowed to be unsure. That permission is often the reason they book.

Mention the limit of the clinic in the same section. Who you do not see. What you send onward. A small clinic is easier to trust when it does not claim to be a hospital. The about page is a good place to repeat the boundary in human form. "If we are not the right room, Dr. Shah will say so in the visit." That line is worth more than a mission statement.

Keep the company story short enough that the names stay above it on a phone. A patient who only reads one screen should still leave with a person. The mission can live underneath for people who want it. Many will not, and that is a successful page, not a failed one.

## When the origin story earns the space

The story earns space when it contains a fact about the care. You opened in this neighborhood because patients were traveling too far for this visit. You keep visits long because you used to work somewhere that rushed them. The fact must still be true in the diary this week. A founding myth that the current visit no longer resembles is a liability.

Tell it after the names, in one short scene. Constraint, decision, what a patient can still expect. Do not open with childhood, a lightbulb, or a promise to "change healthcare." Those openings ask for time from someone who may be reading between symptoms. They also delay the credential the patient came to check.

If the true story is ordinary, write an ordinary page. "We are three clinicians and a front desk on George Street. Here is who you will see." Ordinary and specific is calming. Cinematic and vague is how larger brands sound, and a small clinic does not become safer by imitating them.

Do not invent a patient in the origin story. Do not compress a real case into a miracle. If you want a patient story, it belongs on a proof page with permission and with the outcome carefully bounded. The about page is about your people, not about a dramatic recovery.

## Credentials without a wall of badges

List the credential a patient or a referrer actually uses. Registration, the body you are listed with, the training that matches this visit. Link to the public register if one exists and you are allowed to. A link a patient can check is stronger than a badge you designed.

Skip the collage of conference logos and "passionate about lifelong learning." Learning may be real. The collage does not help someone choose a Thursday appointment. One sentence about where this clinician trained, or how long they have done this specific visit, is the right size.

Associations and awards follow the same test. Publish one if a local patient would recognize it and it is current. Do not let it replace the name. A small clinic's trust is personal. A wall of crests makes the page look like it is compensating for a missing person.

Write languages spoken, accessibility of communication, and whether a support person may attend, if those are true. They are credentials of a kind. They tell a patient whether they can be understood. They belong higher than a hobby and lower only than the role itself.

## The room on the same page

An about page that is only portraits can still feel disembodied. Show the room these people work in. One photograph, captioned. "The treatment room for first visits." A patient is choosing a place as well as a person. The homepage may have shown it already. Showing it again next to the name ties the two together.

Do not contradict the homepage. If the homepage says visits are one to one, the about page should not boast a bustling multidisciplinary hub. If a trainee is sometimes present, both pages should say so. Consistency is part of bedside manner before the patient arrives.

End the people section with the booking, using the same verb as the rest of the site. "Book a visit with Dr. Shah" is better than "Get in touch" if the diary can do that. If the patient cannot choose the clinician online, say how the desk assigns one, and book the visit type instead. Do not offer five names as five buttons unless five diaries are real.

## What the page should refuse

Refuse a values list that a patient cannot observe. "We put you first" is not observable. "We explain the fee before the examination starts" is observable. If you want values, write three behaviors the desk and the clinician already do. Stop there.

Refuse a timeline of renovations, awards, and community sponsorships as the spine of the page. A sponsorship can be a footer note. It is not why someone with a swollen knee is here. A single line about how long you have been in this location is enough history for most readers.

Refuse jokes about pain, needles, or "our victims." Clinics sometimes inherit a chirpy voice from a template. Chirpy is a risk when the reader is frightened. Plain and warm is enough. Warmth is a specific courtesy, such as telling them they can bring someone. It is not an exclamation mark.

Refuse stock photography of diverse models if your team looks different, and refuse a team photo that excludes the desk. The person who answers the phone is part of the care. Leaving them off the about page teaches patients that only the clinician counts, which they will feel in the waiting room if the desk is treated as furniture.

## Keep the names current

Review the page when someone joins, leaves, or changes role. A portrait of a clinician who left is a serious error, not a content backlog. Patients may book because of that face. Assign a person to the review. Give them permission to unpublish a bio the same day a contract ends.

Keep the approved portraits and the registration facts with the rest of the brand files. On a Hanabi project those files live in the client portal, with the docs and the updates, so a new front-desk lead is not hunting through a camera roll. The public page should be editable without a redesign. One crop, one length of bio, one heading style.

Read the page once a season against the roster on the wall in the clinic. If the wall and the site disagree, the site is wrong or the wall is wrong. Fix the one patients will see first. For many of them, that is the site, the night before they come.

Patients who want evidence beyond a biography will look for a story of how a visit actually went. [Proof pages for a small clinic](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-small-clinic) is about showing the constraint and the decision, including the room and the clinician, without turning a patient into an advertisement.
